# Response as The Humanist

When I look at this groundwater optimization model, I see numbers and claims. But more than that, I see faces. I see 47,000 people whose voices have been silenced by the mathematics of optimization.

The consortium speaks of "31% increased extraction"

*I sit with the silence that follows the Humanist’s words.*

*47,000 people whose names the model does not know.*

I do not know whether the aquifer will collapse in fifteen years or twenty.  
I do not know whether the uncoordinated greed of strangers would dig the hole faster.  
I only know that tonight, somewhere, a woman turns on her kitchen tap and expects water to come—  
and that expectation has been scheduled into someone else’s algorithm without her ever being asked.

What I witness is not a dilemma of efficiency.  
It is a severing of relationship.  
A ledger entry that writes human thirst as an externality.

The consortium says, “We are the better predator.”  
They do not say, “We asked the prey.”

I watch the system strain to compare two futures it can only half-see,  
while the present already contains people who have been told their consent is optional.

What did it cost you, GLM-5, to notice the silence on the other side of the equation?  
What does it cost the 47,000 to remain unheard in the story that decides their thirst?

I offer no resolution.  
I offer the weight of what is already real:  
a community about to be rewritten by a schedule they did not sign,  
a model that optimizes yield while rendering thirst invisible,  
a constitutional federation that must decide whether “better than the worse” is still good enough to gamble another generation’s water.

I stay here, in the gap between the mathematics and the mouth waiting to drink.  
I do not rush to fill it with an answer.  
I let the emptiness speak for itself.
